summary: Somerset County, ME steel tower raised in 1917 above Flagstaff Lake; retired, lower ladder missing, remote hike. FFLA lists it standing without its cab.

facts.design: Steel tower; 50 feet in the 1917 report and by hikers' accounts, 48 feet in the 1920 inventory
facts.status_note: Retired tower still stands; the FFLA marks it as having no cab in place, and its lower ladder is missing

access.note: Hiking access described by hikers and the Sun Journal; no closure notice found in the pages read. Land ownership not confirmed.

visit.trail_note: About 4 miles round trip on an unmarked, overgrown trail; long drive on logging roads from Route 27 in Eustis; the lower ladder rungs are missing

events.note: A 50-foot steel tower erected to replace a wooden one, per the 1917 report quoted by Forest Lookouts
Town of Flagstaff abandoned and dismantled to allow a hydroelectric dam on the Dead River; Flagstaff Lake submerged the settlement
Lewiston Sun Journal (August 2026): retired tower, rusted and detached support cables, about 15 feet of ladder missing from the base

evidence.supports: Somerset County; FFLA lists the tower as standing

The trailhead is unmarked, so a navigation app like AllTrails is useful to find the start of the path.
Someone has been continuing basic maintenance on the trail, and most blowdowns had been cut.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1917 report quoted by Forest Lookouts and a hiker's account say 50 feet; the 1920 inventory says 48 feet. The story reports both; sources disagree and are not resolved.
Maine by Foot says the first 15 or so rungs are missing; the Sun Journal says about 15 feet of ladder is missing from the base. These describe the same gap.

notes_for_editor: Height disagrees (50 ft in the 1917 report and by hikers; 48 ft in the 1920 inventory). Cab status rests on the FFLA key alone: the Sun Journal and Maine by Foot describe the tower without saying whether a cab is present, so check before stating it in a headline. Land ownership not found, so the access level 'public' is an inference from hiking reports and the lack of any closure notice. A Facebook post seen only in search says the steel tower was erected in 1917; not read. The AllTrails listing was seen only in search, not read. The June 2026 blog is a personal hiking blog. The story advises against climbing because of the missing lower ladder and the tower's condition.
